newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: MAN DIES IN VIOLENT NSW STORMS
A 21 year old man was killed and a house destroyed during violent storms in New South Wales last night.
Ambulance sources say the man died when a tree was blown onto a car on the Pacific Highway north of Raymond Terrace.
Meanwhile, Fire Brigade officers say a house was destroyed by strong winds at Dungog last night.
Authorities say most of the storm damage last night was concentrated in the Dungog, Gloucester and Stroud areas, with numerous reports of roof damage at Forster.
Stroud area State Emergency Services Controller, John Kopo, says crews have been working throughout the night to assist people whose homes were damaged.
REITH SAYS WAGE RISE OFFER IS FAIR

Federal Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, says the ACTU's wage claim compared to the Government's would lead to higher interest rates, higher inflation and higher unemployment. Mr Reith says the Government's proposed eight dollar a week wage rise for low paid workers is fair, without jeopardising low inflation.
The Government's offering eight dollars a week for each of the next three years for workers on awards less than average weekly ordinary time earnings.
But the ACTU, which is seeking 20 dollars a week for low paid workers, describes the offer as miserable and inadequate.
ACTU Assistant Secretary Greg Combet, says because the Government's offer is lower than inflation, workers will be worse off.
TOBACCO REPORT TO BE CHALLENGED TODAY
A National Health and Medical Research Council report on passive smoking will today be the subject of a Federal Court challenge in Canberra.
The report recomends that State and Territory Governments consider broader public health measures to protect Australians, especially children from the risks associated with passive smoking.
It says at least 3,000 children are taken to hospital each year with asthma caused by tobacco smoke.

But the Tobacco Institute, Phillip Morris and Rothmans, argue the report fails to take into account 75 scientific reports, which show there's inadequate evidence to establish a causal relationship between passive smoking and illness.
ANTI-ASIAN FEELING COULD COST AUSTRALIA
The Malaysian Consul says Australia's still "on the ropes" in terms of what the Asian business community sees as anti-Asian feeling.
Former Northern Territory Chief Minister and former Queensland Liberal Party President, Paul Everingham, wants the Federal Government to introduce a public awareness campaign.
Mr Everingham says he's received feedback that racist attitudes in Australia are causing concern in the region.
COLLIERY MAY REOPEN AFTER DEATH OF FOUR
Managers of the Gretley Colliery in Newcastle will today review when the mine's likely to be reopened.
Four miners died in an accident at the mine last week, and management has not yet determined whether the colliery is now safe.

The New South Wales Government, mine owners Oakbridge, the coal miners' union, and the coroner are investigating why the tunnel in which the men were working was flooded with water from a disused mine shaft.
The ABC understands it's normal practice to establish a 100 metre buffer zone between new mining areas and old workings.
Test drillings are also used when working near former mine shafts to check whether water or gas are present.
EUTHANASIA DOCTOR TO APPEAR BEFORE CORONER
Pro-euthanasia doctor, Philip Nitschke, has admitted prescribing two patients methadone, but says he did so for pain relief and doesn't believe he acted negligently.
Doctor Nitschke is to appear before a coroner in Darwin today, following the drug-related death of the two men.
Unlike any state in Australia, in the Northern Territory it's illegal to prescribe methadone for addiction.
Doctor Nitschke says he believes it's reasonable and legal to treat pain which may co-exist with addiction by using methadone or other strong narcotic relievers.
GAMBLING CONFERENCE IN ADELAIDE TODAY
Some of the world's leading academics and researchers on gambling, will take part in a national conference in Adelaide today.
It's the annual conference of the National Association of Gambling Studies.
The Association's President Vin Glenn says issues to be discussed during the next four days, will include the prevelance of problem gambling and its link to suicides.
He says the conference will also co-incide with the release of a Federal Government report on gambling.
